Satiation Is Not Enough

In brief One hope about superintelligent AI is that a machine built to want only so much would stop expanding once it had enough. In a model of conflict over a chain of gains, I show that wanting only so much is not enough when humanity cannot promise never to switch the machine off or build a rival. Each further gain can still make the machine safer; when that capped goal has positive value, defeat is not certain, more holdings never raise the risk of being defeated by a strike while the top holding lowers it, and fighting is cheap enough, safety alone makes climbing pay better than stopping. In the model, wanting only so much (satiation) suffices at every attack cost under further conditions—such as when more holdings buy no extra safety, when the stopping point is calm and no one builds rivals, or in some cases where grabbing more would unite humanity in alarm or where no community gains from striking—and a high enough attack cost also makes the machine stop. I use no measurements from real AI systems or real societies to establish these results.

Part 1. A machine that has enough may still want to be safe

A side that is gaining power struggles to settle disputes peacefully. It cannot credibly promise not to use tomorrow’s strength to demand more tomorrow (Powell 2006). This is the commitment problem.

Smith and Stam (2001; see also Smith 1998b) modelled war as a run of battles over a chain of forts, where each battle won moves the front one fort along. They argue that when every extra fort adds the same amount to a side’s payoff, no deal that hands over forts is reached in the equilibria they examine, patterns of choices in which no side gains by changing its own. Each fort won only sharpens the appetite or the capacity for the next.

Four years later, Smith and Stam (2005) named a possible way out in a remark with no formal model behind it: “if the value of additional forts drops off sufficiently then nations can commit not to increase demands following territorial gains.” In The War Baseline, my paper setting out the commitment problem and the war model this series builds on, I call that way out the heartland condition.

Applied to AI, the heartland condition expresses a hope. Suppose a superintelligence were built or trained to want only so much. Its goal pays it an amount each period that depends on its holdings. That amount stops growing once it holds enough resources or territory, and it drops to zero if the machine is defeated. I call such a goal satiable, and the holding where it stops growing the satiation point. The hope is that a machine like this could credibly promise to stop acquiring.

The trouble is that a machine with enough still wants to survive to enjoy it. Humanity may be unable to credibly promise never to pull the plug, or never to build a rival machine to displace it. If so, more holdings may make the machine safer even after they add nothing to its goal. Expansion for security and the wish to preserve oneself are familiar ideas in words, reviewed in The War Baseline and examined in Ends, Rank and Conflict, my paper on whether actors with limited aims can rest satisfied. My contribution is a formal model that joins a satiable goal to a risk of being struck that more holdings reduce.

The model gives several results that do not follow at a glance from how it is set up:

  • If the goal is worth something and the next fort lowers a strike’s chance of success without eliminating it, the safety gain from settling one fort higher can first rise and then fall as strikes become more frequent.
  • In a fuller game where humanity also chooses, an equilibrium with peace at the satiation point, in rules that depend only on the current holding, needs only that no community gains from striking on its own at that point itself. This holds even when holdings above it would draw strikes (proved on paper).
  • One calibration, a particular set of payoff choices, uses an imperfect plug and makes both pulling the plug and building a rival costly. When communities choose strategically whether to build and all use the same strategy, each community’s chance of building is at most a fixed number divided by the number of communities, once there are many. Adding communities then does not by itself force the machine’s removal.
  • In that fuller game, a peaceful stop and an attack driven by human alarm can both be equilibria at the same attack cost.

These rest on simpler results: a one-step test for stopping, a split of the gain from one more fort into a goal part and a safety part, and an account of how a shutdown that needs everyone combines with a rival that needs only one.

I pose five questions:

  1. If a machine’s goals were satiable, could it stop acquiring, or does the wish to keep what it has keep it acquiring?
  2. With no outside threat, how fast must the appetite for more fall off before stopping pays?
  3. Does satiation still make stopping pay when holdings also buy safety against strikes?
  4. When humanity is a player with promises of its own to keep, when do both sides stop?
  5. Does adding communities of fixed capability help or hurt restraint compared with humanity acting as one?

My thesis is that satiation alone does not deliver restraint, even granting a satiable goal that is enjoyed only while the machine survives. I call the chance of defeat by a strike in a period the strike risk. In the stopping result, the capped goal has positive value and the machine can survive at the proposed stop. If the risk never rises on the way up and is lower at the top than at every holding from the proposed stop to just below the top, satiation fails to make stopping best when fighting is cheap enough. The general stopping result takes that risk as given. When humanity’s choices produce it, it can persist in equilibrium too. The examples put the satiation point at holding 3. With fixed positive chances that communities build rivals, some computed equilibria keep the strike risk positive from there through holding 6. With both ways of striking chosen strategically, an example with high human stakes and many communities gives a positive strike risk at holdings 3 and 4, with holding 5 safe.

The technical paper gives the formal definitions, exact conditions and proofs in its appendices. Its analytical results, up to the fuller game near the end, are checked by a proof-checking program (Lean 4), subject to conditions and exceptions it records. Such a program confirms that each conclusion follows from the stated assumptions, not that the assumptions hold in the world. The fuller game’s results are computed or proved on paper, and the numerical examples are computed by scripts.

Part 2. In the model, each step up costs an attack and may buy safety

Four things come from earlier work

I take four things as given from The War Baseline.

First, a side that is gaining power cannot credibly promise not to exploit its future strength. Large, rapid shifts in power can produce war even when nothing is hidden (Powell 2006). Drawing on Fearon (1996, cited via Powell 2006), Powell (2006) states a condition under which peace breaks down: what the rising side can secure next period, scaled down because it comes a period later, minus what it secures now, exceeds what is left over once both sides’ present guarantees are met. On my reading of Powell (2006, 192–194), a second mechanism matters here. A state may choose to fight today when living under a threat over time costs more than fighting to end it.

Second, I use a one-sided version of the chain-of-forts model. In Smith and Stam’s examples, no deal that pays in forts is reached in the equilibria they study. They argue this from the structure of continuation values, the value of going on from each holding, rather than proving it as a general theorem. On their argument, because the value of going on rises strictly with each fort held, a fort handed over today only sharpens the receiver’s appetite or capacity for the next. In their examples, each fort either adds the same amount to a side’s payoff or raises its chance of winning the next battle.

Third, I take the heartland condition from the single sentence of Smith and Stam (2005) quoted above. The formal model in that work values a prize, not forts. The remark about forts losing value is an aside it does not model.

Fourth, I assume, as in The War Baseline, that humanity cannot credibly promise never to build a rival machine.

The chain of forts

The model follows one side, the gainer, which here is the machine, up a chain of forts numbered from 0 to a top fort. As in Smith and Stam (2004), a fort stands for a discrete step in strategic capacity. For AI, read it as a step of computing power or capability. I call reaching the top fort domination. In cases where strikes and rivals cannot succeed at the top, it represents the machine disarming those threats. There is also a state of defeat, worth nothing forever.

Each period below the top, the machine chooses whether to attack, that is, to bid for the next fort. An attack costs a fixed amount, the attack cost, and succeeds with a fixed chance. That cost is zero or more, and the chance of success is above zero. If it succeeds, the machine moves up one fort. If it fails, the machine stays where it is and loses no forts. Holdings only ratchet upward: capability once acquired is not lost when a bid for the next step fails.

Each holding yields a value of zero or more in every period the machine starts undefeated, including a period in which a strike defeats it. The goal is satiated from a holding when forts beyond it add nothing to that value. I assume the goal is a flow, enjoyed while the machine is alive and lost at defeat. It is not a finished task that stays banked once achieved. Everything this guide says about safety rests on protecting that flow.

The other side cannot commit not to strike. Each period it strikes with some frequency, and a strike succeeds with a chance that depends on how many forts the machine holds. A successful strike defeats the machine. The strike risk at a holding (the technical paper’s strike hazard) is that frequency times that chance. At a given holding, the model treats the risk of defeat by a strike as independent of whether the machine’s own attack succeeds. Forts carry safety value whenever the strike’s chance of success falls as holdings rise. If that chance is zero at the top, domination ends the threat.

Two more assumptions matter. The machine evaluates uncertain outcomes by weighting each payoff by its chance and adding the results. It also has a fixed patience, the share of a period’s value it still counts when that value comes one period later. Patience lies strictly between zero and one. And events within a period run in a fixed order. The machine collects its value and pays for any attack. Then the strike is resolved. Then, if the machine survived and attacked, the attack’s outcome decides where it starts next period. Figure 1 lays out one period below the top, step by step, in the order the model sets.

The machine must survive this period’s strike before an attack can move it up. If the higher holding is safer, a successful attack brings that safety from the next period on. The reverse order is analysed only in two narrow remarks. Information is also complete. In Smith and Stam’s later models, fighting reveals information about the odds of battle (Smith and Stam 2004) or settles a disagreement about the costs of fighting (Smith and Stam 2005). Here nobody learns anything by fighting. Figure 2 draws this set-up as a chain of forts, in the case of lower strike risk at higher holdings.

A best policy is not a promise

A policy here is a rule that says, for each holding, whether to attack. For any such rule, working backward from the top gives a single value at each holding. That value combines the current payoff with the discounted value expected from the next period on. The best value at each holding can be worked out backward from the top, one fort at a time. By a standard argument, the best rule that depends only on the current holding is also best among rules that use the history available to the machine, or that mix finitely many rules by chance.

I say stopping at a holding is the machine’s best policy when never attacking again is optimal there. Ties count: if stopping and attacking are worth exactly the same, I count it as a stop. The strike risk is fixed and does not respond to anything the machine announces. So this tests whether stopping pays against a threat that keeps coming. It is not a test of two promises kept together.

The distinction runs through the rest of the guide. In the first half of the technical paper, the other side is simply a fixed strike risk, so the machine faces a decision, not a game. Later, humanity has payoffs and chooses whether to pull a plug or build a rival. Even there, “stopping is the best policy” still means best against a strike risk taken as given. Separate results say when both sides’ choices are best replies to each other.

Two bodies of work meet here without settling the question

In international relations, scholars divide over whether states with limited aims can rest satisfied once their core interests are met. The other side of that debate holds that anarchy compels even satisfied states to keep acquiring power for security, a debate examined in Ends, Rank and Conflict. In AI research, arguments about instrumental convergence hold that an agent pursuing almost any final goal has a reason to acquire resources and to protect itself from being switched off, a baseline reviewed in The War Baseline. Both literatures state the security logic in words. The model puts it in a form where results can be proved.

Part 3. In the model, the machine stops only when one more step is not worth one attack

The basic test is simple. Stopping at a holding is the best policy exactly when one more attack is not worth its cost. This is proved for any fixed strike risk (the technical paper’s Proposition 1).

More precisely, take the gain from moving up one fort and then doing the best possible from there, rather than staying put forever. Discount that gain for patience and for the chance of surviving this period’s strike. Multiply it by the chance the attack succeeds. Stopping is the best policy if and only if the result is no more than the attack cost.

A simpler check follows from this. Compare staying at this holding forever with staying one fort up forever, weighted the same way; call that difference the one-step gain. For stopping to be best, the one-step gain must not exceed the attack cost. The check is necessary but not sufficient, because a machine may want to pass through the next fort to reach more valuable forts higher up. Figure 3 sets the quick check beside the exact test it is drawn from.

There is a stronger result. The one-step check holds at every holding from here to the top exactly when the machine would stop wherever it stood from here up (Proposition 2). Stopping at a single holding asks for less than that. It can be the best policy even when the machine would attack from some higher holding that it never reaches, because it stopped first.

The gain from one more fort has a goal part and a safety part

As an analogy that is mine and not the technical paper’s: a farmer who has all the land they want may still buy the next field. They do not mean to farm it. They mean to keep a hostile neighbour further from the house.

The model makes this exact. The raw difference between staying one fort up forever and staying at this holding forever splits into two pieces (Proposition 3, proved). To get the one-step gain, scale that raw difference by patience, the chance of surviving this period and the chance the attack succeeds. Apply the same three adjustments to each piece to get its weighted contribution. The goal part (the technical paper’s end term) is the extra value the next fort adds each period, counted over the machine’s discounted expected life at the higher holding. The safety part (its security term) is the value the machine already enjoys each period, multiplied by patience and by how much the next fort raises the chance of surviving a period, and scaled by the discounted expected lives at both holdings.

Satiation sets the goal part to zero at every holding from the satiation point up. It leaves the safety part untouched. The safety part is strictly positive whenever all three of these hold:

  • the satiated goal is worth something;
  • strikes happen;
  • the next fort lowers a strike’s chance of success.

If the goal is worth something and strikes occur, taking a fort that makes strikes more likely to succeed gives a negative safety part.

The safety part need not grow steadily as strikes become more frequent. Suppose the goal at that holding is worth something and the next fort lowers a strike’s chance of success without removing it. Then the raw safety part rises with strike frequency while strikes are rare, below a threshold, and falls once strike frequency passes that threshold, because very frequent strikes shorten the machine’s expected life at both holdings and shrink the value of whatever it holds. A turn is possible only if the machine counts a payoff next period at more than half its face value. Whether the turn comes before strikes are certain to occur also depends on the chances that a strike succeeds at the two holdings. Figure 4 sets the case with a turning point beside the case without one.

What happens at the last step into domination? When domination ends the threat entirely, the raw safety part of the last step rises with strike frequency across the whole range. The weighted gain from that step also counts the chance of surviving this period’s strike. That weighted gain can still turn down when strikes are very frequent, and it vanishes when a strike is certain to come and to succeed every period.

In the technical paper’s computed example, a strike comes in one period out of ten (a frequency of 0.1). There, the weighted goal part drops to zero at the satiation point while the weighted safety part rises toward domination. Past satiation, each further fort is worth more the closer the machine comes to ending the threat. That acceleration is a property of the example’s numbers, not a general theorem.

Part 4. With no threat, stopping needs the appetite for the next fort to fall low enough

With no threat at all, the safety part vanishes, and the model gives a stopping version of the heartland condition (Theorem B, proved). It holds in this model, where a failed attack loses no forts. It uses one more condition. From the next fort onward, each successive fort adds no more to the goal than the previous one added.

Start with the extra value per period from the next fort. Count that stream from next period onward, discount it for patience and weight it by the chance the attack succeeds. Stopping is best exactly when the result is no more than the cost of one attack. Later forts never add more, so meeting this test at one holding means no higher holding tempts the machine either.

Two consequences show what this rate demands. The first is about patience. For any fixed positive extra value from the next fort, a patient enough machine does not stop. This part needs only the absence of a threat, not the assumption that later forts add less. Without fort loss on a failed attack, a patient enough machine keeps going while the next fort adds anything at all. Figure 5 plots the no-threat test’s cutoff against patience.

The second is about a next fort that adds nothing. If it adds nothing and later forts add no more than that, stopping is the best policy at every attack cost, zero included. Two cautions apply. This is weaker than satiation, since later forts could even lower the goal’s value. And a next fort that adds nothing is not enough on its own. If the fort after it brings a large jump in value and fighting is cheap, the machine attacks to pass through the next fort and take the one beyond.

Both the patience result and the failure of restraint at zero cost in Part 5 rest on one assumption: holdings only ratchet up, and a failed attack loses no forts. A failed attack then leaves the machine exactly where it was, so the attack cost bears the whole burden of deterrence. As patience approaches its limit, the counted value of the next fort grows without bound against a fixed fee. At zero cost, attacking is free whenever winning improves safety.

A risk of losing forts on a failed attack, or a strike risk that attacks themselves provoke, would add a further cost of attacking. I do not derive the stopping condition for that case.

Part 5. Satiation is enough when more holdings buy no safety, and not enough when they do and fighting is cheap

When more holdings buy no safety, a satiated machine stops at any cost

Satiation by itself delivers restraint when expanding does not make the machine safer (Theorem A, proved). This holds when the goal is satiated from a holding at a value of zero or more, and the strike risk never falls as holdings rise from there. Then, at every attack cost including zero, the machine stops at every holding from there up.

That covers three situations: no threat at all; a threat that is the same at every holding, so that not even domination lowers it; and a threat that grows as the machine takes more forts. If domination ends the threat, a risk that never falls on the way up must already be zero. So the second and third situations arise only when domination does not end the threat.

The result reaches down to zero cost only because ties count as stops. With no threat or a flat one, a satiated machine is indifferent between staying and attacking when attacking is free. A stricter rule, demanding a strict preference for stopping, would need a positive attack cost there.

When more holdings buy safety, cheap fighting blocks stopping

When holdings buy safety and domination lowers the threat, satiation fails to deliver restraint whenever fighting is cheap (Theorem C, proved). This holds at a holding below the top when four conditions hold from there up:

  1. the goal is satiated at a positive value;
  2. more holdings never raise the strike risk;
  3. domination is safer than every holding from the proposed stopping point to just below the top;
  4. no holding from there up makes defeat certain.

Then there is a positive blocking cost: at any attack cost below it, stopping is not the best policy, and at zero cost it never is. If the conditions hold from the satiation point up, a single positive blocking cost covers every holding from the satiation point to just below the top.

Each condition does work. Given the second, the third needs only that domination be safer than the fort just below it. The fourth then needs only that defeat not be certain at the stopping point. It is needed because certain defeat comes this period, before any attack could move the machine up. Attacking then ties stopping if it is free and pays less if it costs anything. The second is needed because a path to domination through a much more dangerous fort can deter the machine from starting the climb, even when attacking is free. The technical paper has a small example of this.

A high enough attack cost still lets the machine stop

Theorem C blocks stopping only below the blocking cost. It does not say a satiated machine can never stop short of domination. At higher costs the basic test of Part 3 decides, and a high enough attack cost makes stopping the best policy even when the safety value is active. Call the lowest attack cost at which stopping is best the break-even cost. Under Theorem C’s conditions it is at least the blocking cost. Figure 6 sets the blocking cost and the break-even cost side by side.

The computed example shows how the break-even cost at the satiation point, holding 3, moves with strike frequency. It is an illustration, not a test:

How often a strike comes Break-even attack cost at holding 3
never 0
0.01 0.087
0.05 0.354
0.1 0.563
0.2 0.769

When a strike comes in one period out of ten, each attack must cost more than half of a period’s full satiated value before the machine stops at its satiation point. In this model a period, the attack cost and the goal’s value have no calibrated meaning for AI. So how large the attack cost is, relative to the goal’s value, for any real AI system is unknown.

Two readings of older work

Two links to the conflict literature are my own readings, not claims of the cited authors. On the first, Theorem C carries Powell’s (2006) second commitment mechanism into the chain of forts. The machine fights because living under the strike risk costs more in expected goal value than paying to climb to domination and end the threat.

On the second, the split into goal and safety parts shows why Smith and Stam’s (2001) argument against fort-transfer deals changes here. Their argument relies on the value of going on rising strictly with each fort, because each fort adds the same amount. Satiation removes that rise in the goal. The safety part restores it whenever holdings reduce the threat.

Part 6. When humanity chooses, peace needs humanity not to want the machine gone too badly

Humanity has two ways to strike

In the second half of the technical paper, the gainer is the machine and humanity’s choices produce the strike risk. Humanity is made of one or more communities. Each community gets some value per period while the machine holds a given number of forts. If the machine is removed, the model assigns the community a value per period from then on. All communities share the same patience.

Humanity can strike in two ways:

  • Pulling the plug needs every community. If all of them pull, each pays a cost, and each community’s part succeeds independently with some chance. If every part succeeds, the plug removes the machine with a chance that depends on its holdings.
  • Building a rival needs only one community. Any community that pays the cost of building one removes the machine that period with some chance. The cost of either kind of strike can be zero.

Where a result needs it, both chances never rise as the machine holds more, and domination disarms both.

A stopping point that is safe enough lets the machine stop

Humanity’s willingness to strike may differ across holdings, so the strike risk need not fall steadily as the machine climbs. Two proved results cover a satiated machine facing a risk of any shape. Both use the same bound. At a given holding, attacking until the machine moves up cannot pay more than the better of staying put forever and starting one fort higher.

The first (Theorem A′) applies when the stopping point is at least as safe as every holding above it, domination included. Then stopping there is the best policy at every attack cost. In particular, if the strike risk at the stopping point is zero, stopping is best at every cost, whatever the risk above. This needs less than Theorem A, but it concludes only that stopping at that one holding is best. It is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one, since a high enough attack cost makes any stop below the top the best policy.

The second (Theorem D) applies if domination is safer than the stopping point and the stopping point is at least as safe as every holding in between. Then the machine’s only temptation is to climb all the way. Stopping is best exactly when attacking at every holding up to domination is worth no more than staying put.

Humanity’s promise not to strike

Now take humanity’s side while the machine stays put at some holding. A single strike does not pay exactly when its chance of success, times the discounted and permanent gain from having the machine gone, is no larger than its cost (Proposition 4, proved). That same condition makes never striking humanity’s best policy, against all its possible policies, while the machine stays put. When it holds, humanity’s promise not to strike such a machine is credible.

The peace profile

Put both sides together. The technical paper’s peace profile is a pattern of play in which, at every holding from the satiation point to the top, the machine does not attack and no community pulls or builds. Each side’s choice depends only on the machine’s current holding (the technical paper’s stationary Markov strategies). An equilibrium is a set of choices in which no side gains by changing its own.

When domination disarms both ways of striking, no player can gain by a single change of action at any holding from the satiation point up to the top exactly when, at each of those holdings below the top, the condition for the number of communities holds (Theorem P, proved):

  • with a single community, neither pulling the plug nor building a rival is worth its cost;
  • with two or more communities, building a rival is not worth its cost for any community.

With two or more communities no plug condition is needed. A lone pull while the others refrain cannot work and costs zero or more, so the plug side of peace holds by coordination alone. If pulling is free, removal is preferred and the plug can work, refraining merely ties pulling when others hold back and does worse if everyone else pulls.

That coordination comes with a catch. With two or more communities, peace can sit alongside a second equilibrium in which every community pulls. When no community builds a rival, that needs the chance that an all-community pull succeeds, times how much each community’s discounted future improves if the machine is gone, to cover the cost of pulling. Where both equilibria exist, plug restraint amounts to choosing the one with no pulling. Part 8 uses the opposite rule.

A hand proof (Lemma 6) shows that these conditions make the peace profile hold up if play starts at any holding from the satiation point through domination. The technical term is a subgame-perfect equilibrium.

In a fuller dynamic game, each side’s decision accounts for what can happen in later periods. In it, the machine and every community choose at the same time each period, and each side’s value of going on is worked out rather than assumed. Its results are computed or proved on paper.

In that game, peace at the satiation point needs less than the full peace profile (Proposition 7, proved on paper). An equilibrium of this kind, with both sides holding back at the satiation point, exists if and only if no community gains from striking on its own at that holding itself. It can coexist with strikes at higher holdings, which the machine would reach only by breaking off from peace. Because the strategies depend only on the current holding, these results rule out the machine retaliating after a failed strike and humanity growing alarmed after a failed attack. They say nothing about equilibria in which past events matter. Figure 7 sets the two kinds of peace side by side and marks where each must pass the strike check.

Two consequences follow. First, peace needs humanity not to want a satiated machine gone badly enough to pay for a strike. Satiation solves the machine’s side when nobody strikes. Peace fails on humanity’s side if a community can make a strike on its own and its chance of success, multiplied by the discounted gain from removal, outweighs its cost.

Second, suppose humanity strikes the same way at every holding from the satiation point up. Suppose also that the resulting risk is positive below domination, short of certain at the stopping point, never rising, and zero at domination. If the satiated goal is worth something, that risk meets Theorem C’s conditions, and then the machine will not stop either when fighting is cheap. In the technical paper I identify which of these conditions the dynamic-game examples meet.

Part 7. With many communities, a shared plug falls apart while rivals persist

A plug needs all, a rival needs one

As an analogy of my own: the plug is like a vote that must be unanimous, while a rival is like a lottery in which any one winning ticket is enough.

Suppose every community tries to pull the plug, and each also has a fixed chance of fielding a rival that removes the machine. The two channels move in opposite directions as communities are added. I call the plug an AND technology. Every community’s part must work, so its chance of success never rises with the number of communities, and it shrinks geometrically, by a fixed fraction with each added community, if each part can fail. A rival is an OR technology. One is enough, so the combined rival risk never falls as communities are added. In this independent-channels model, the chance the machine survives both kinds of strike is the chance the plug fails multiplied by the chance all rivals fail. Figure 8 plots both chances against the number of communities, using values chosen only for the drawing.

With every community pulling at every size, the combined risk changes direction at most once as communities are added (Proposition 6, proved). It can fall while the weakening plug dominates, then rise once multiplying rivals dominate. Once adding a community stops lowering the risk, adding more never lowers it again, provided no community is certain to field a rival that removes the machine. And when rivals are possible and each community’s part of the plug can fail, there is a number of communities beyond which the risk never falls.

When there are no rivals, the risk never rises as communities are added. The risk never falls if every community’s part of the plug always works. It also never falls if adding a second community already leaves the combined risk unchanged or raises it. This single turn holds only while every community always pulls. Once communities drop out of the plug where it no longer pays, the plug’s share of the risk vanishes and the risk can turn again.

As communities multiply, the plug coalition dissolves

I started from a conjecture. Suppose pulling the plug required the cooperation of every human community, a game of one machine against many rather than one against one. Then perhaps the difficulty of coordinating that many would by itself make humanity’s restraint more credible, and the machine’s stop easier to sustain.

On the plug side, part of this is immediate. With two or more communities, no single one gains by pulling while the others refrain, since a lone pull achieves nothing and costs zero or more. So restraint from the plug is always one equilibrium, held up by coordination alone. In the fixed-rival game, if pulling is free, removal is preferred, the plug can work and rivals might fail, pulling can do better than holding back and can never do worse. That does not establish the conjecture, because all communities pulling together can also be an equilibrium. Where it is, plug restraint means choosing one equilibrium among several. Powell (2006) warns that accounts resting on coordination across multiple equilibria are weak.

Whether everyone pulling is an equilibrium turns on a community’s stake in removal. This is a summary number for how much its discounted future improves if the machine is gone. In the dynamic game, the stake also reflects the machine’s chance of advancing after a failed strike. Hold the chance of rivals fixed. Then pulling is each community’s best reply to everyone else pulling if and only if three things multiplied together cover the cost of pulling: the plug’s chance of success, the chance no rival removes the machine that period, and the stake.

What bears out the conjecture is how the condition without rivals—that the plug’s chance of success times the stake covers the cost of pulling, which the three-part condition also requires—behaves as communities are added (proved). With a non-negative stake held fixed, if that condition fails at some number of communities, it fails at every larger number. If each community’s part of the plug can fail and pulling costs something, it fails once there are enough communities. Beyond that point pulling loses whatever the others do, so no community pulls in any equilibrium, including ones where communities choose at random.

Rivals run the other way

On the rival side, adding communities has the opposite effect. One rival is enough, so peace needs every community to hold back. Suppose each community independently sets out to build a rival with a fixed chance, its building propensity. Whenever that propensity is above zero and below one, the chance that no community builds falls toward zero as communities are added. I call this the fixed-propensity benchmark.

Now suppose communities choose strategically, with common stakes, rival costs and rival success chances held fixed as communities are added. In the peace profile, each community’s rival condition does not involve the number of communities at all. Peace then holds at every number of communities from two up, or at none. A single community must also meet the plug condition, which can fail where the rival condition holds.

These results have three limits of scope. They add communities of fixed capability; splitting a fixed total capability among more communities is not analysed. A rival’s success counts only as removing the machine. Humanity’s payoffs treat removal as leading to a world with no machine, not to a new machine in charge, a case left to Many Machines, my paper on interactions among several machines. And because removal changes payoffs for every community, strategic builders have an incentive to free-ride on one another’s rival projects, as the dynamic game shows.

Rivals alone can block stopping

Once there are enough communities that the plug coalition dissolves, the machine faces a strike risk from rivals alone. Rivals then block stopping when fighting is cheap (Theorem E, proved). In the conditions that follow, count only holdings at or above the proposed stopping point. This holds at a holding below the top, for any number of communities, when:

  • the rival’s chance of success never rises with holdings and is zero at domination;
  • at every holding below the top, each community’s chance of removing the machine with a rival is above zero and below one;
  • the goal is satiated at a positive value.

Then there is a positive blocking cost below which stopping is not the best policy. Even after the plug coalition is gone, independent rivals keep the safety motive alive when fighting is cheap.

How large is that blocking cost as communities multiply? There is a ceiling. Stopping is the best policy whenever the attack cost is at least an amount proportional to the machine’s chance of surviving all the rivals for one period at the stopping point. For a given survival chance, this ceiling is higher when attacks are more likely to succeed, the full goal is worth more per period or the machine is more patient. That ceiling caps both the break-even cost and the blocking cost. In the fixed-propensity benchmark, if each community has a positive chance of removing the machine with a rival at the stopping point and the strike comes first, the ceiling falls by a fixed fraction as each community is added.

It is the ceiling that falls toward zero, not the break-even cost at every step. With a fixed propensity and very many communities, rivals make the risk at the stopping point so high that the machine’s expected life there is short. Heavy discounting for survival then makes safety worth little, so even a small attack cost makes the machine stop. That stop reflects a short expected life, not restraint. Over smaller numbers of communities, though, adding communities can push the rival risk up from near zero into the range where safety is valuable. So the break-even cost need not move in one direction.

Would the other order of events change this? In one case, yes. If the attack came before the strike, consider a machine one fort below domination. A successful attack would reach domination at once, where rivals cannot succeed, and the one-step gain would not vanish as communities are added. It would approach the discounted value of the full satiated goal from next period onward, weighted by the chance that the attack succeeds. I analyse the reverse order only in this special case and in a one-step comparison that holds the value of going on fixed.

The dynamic game revisits the fixed-propensity benchmark (Proposition 8). Under its calibration, the plug is imperfect and costly to pull, and rivals are costly to build. In a symmetric equilibrium, where all communities behave alike, each community’s building propensity is then at most a fixed multiple of one over the number of communities, once there are many. Whether a positive blocking cost survives then depends on the payoffs. Figure 9 previews the dynamic game’s two examples, explained in Part 9, comparing the rivals’ peace condition at holding 3.

Part 8. In the model, tripwires carry the stop only in some cases

Suppose humanity is hard to unite while a machine stays calm at its satiation point, and easier to unite in alarm if it grabs more. That would create a tripwire: a low strike risk at the stopping point and a higher plug risk in an alarm band of holdings above it. The question is whether coordination among many communities produces such a tripwire. A second question is whether it sustains restraint even though domination disarms any coalition. Figure 10 draws this tripwire as the model tests it, with a calm stopping point below the alarm band.

In the model’s version, each community’s stake in removal is low in calm and high in the alarm band. These stakes are held fixed as the number of communities and the rival chances vary, so the alarm band in the first benchmark table below (Table 1) depends on that choice. To turn stakes into a strike risk, the model adopts a selection rule. Humanity coordinates on everyone pulling wherever that is an equilibrium, and nobody pulls where it is not. The plug risk is then zero in calm, positive in the alarm band, and zero at domination. Powell’s (2006) warning about coordination accounts applies here too.

The technical paper’s two benchmark tables (Tables 1 and 2) use fixed propensities and fixed stakes, a game in which communities choose only whether to pull, and this selection rule. The dynamic game revisits both by working out the stakes from the value of going on. Under its calibration, the first table’s tripwire can sustain an equilibrium stop. But attack equilibria can coexist at the same cost. A peaceful stop can also coexist with credible strikes that would come only if the machine broke off from peace.

In the model, four results follow:

  1. A calm stopping point with no rivals is enough. Suppose everyone pulling is not an equilibrium at the satiation point and nobody builds rivals. Then the strike risk there is zero. By Theorem A′, stopping is the best policy at every attack cost. Domination’s disarming of humanity does not undo this, since domination is no safer than a calm point. The calm does the work, and the alarm band above is idle: a risk of zero everywhere gives the same answer. In Table 1, with no rivals, the break-even cost is zero at every number of communities.

  2. In Table 1’s benchmark, with rivals and alarm only above the satiation point, the tripwire carries the stop for a few communities. In Table 1, alarm begins at holding 4, one above the satiation point at holding 3. With rivals present, the stopping point is then less safe than domination, and the basic test of Part 3 decides. Theorem D simplifies that test when holding 3 is the safest holding below domination, but in Table 1 that never happens when rivals are present. At one, two and four communities, holdings above the alarm band carry only a lower rival risk, and from eight communities on the alarm band is empty, leaving only that rival risk at every holding above holding 3. Take one community with a building propensity of 0.2. A risk from rivals alone would give a positive break-even cost by Theorem E, but the alarm band above holding 3 brings it down to zero. Across numbers of communities, in Table 1’s comparison with stakes and building propensities held fixed, the break-even cost does not move in one direction.

  3. With many communities and rivals, the tripwire vanishes. Hold the stakes fixed, and let the plug be imperfect and costly to pull. Once there are enough communities, pulling together ceases to be an equilibrium at every holding. (The dynamic game extends this on paper to stakes that may change with the number of communities but stay under a common limit.) The risk then comes from rivals alone, and under Theorem E’s conditions stopping is not the best policy below a positive blocking cost. The tripwire conjecture fails here. The AND structure dissolves the tripwire, while in the fixed-propensity benchmark the OR structure keeps a rival threat alive. That threat’s ceiling on the blocking cost shrinks toward zero, with the strike coming first in each period. This reflects a short expected life, not restraint, and the dynamic game revisits it for strategic rivals.

  4. In Table 2’s fixed-stake benchmark, alarm that already covers the satiation point drives the machine to climb unless fighting is costly or there are enough communities to dissolve the alarm at the stopping point. With no rivals but alarm starting at holding 1, the satiation point at holding 3 lies inside the alarm band. The machine faces an active plug risk there that falls as it climbs and drops to zero past the band, a case covered by a broader version of Theorem C. The broader result looks for the first higher holding that is safer than every holding passed along the way from the stopping point. In Table 2 the machine climbs from holding 3 unless the attack cost reaches the break-even cost. That cost rises from 1.045 with one community to 3.317 with eight, as the band’s top retreats from holding 5 to holding 3, and drops to 0 at twelve. Yet it already rises from 1.045 to 1.064 between one and two communities while the band stays the same. So linking the rise to the retreat is a reading of computed values, not a proved result.

On that fourth case, two more points matter. In the cases with two, four and eight communities, the climb rests on the selection rule picking everyone pulling at holding 3. If nobody pulls there, the break-even cost is zero by Theorem A′, and the dynamic game has both kinds of equilibrium for these numbers. With one community, the alarm band in the dynamic game need not start at holding 1 with holding 0 calm, because the machine’s prospect of advancing makes pulling worthwhile even at holding 0. Figure 11 shows two equilibria at holding 3 that can coexist at the same attack cost (two, four, eight communities).

The verdict on the tripwire conjecture is mixed:

  • A calm stopping point with no rivals suffices at every cost.
  • In the first table’s benchmark, an alarm band above satiation, with rivals present, carries the stop for a few communities.
  • With many communities and a fixed positive building propensity, the tripwire dissolves and rivals block stopping when fighting is cheap.
  • In the second table’s benchmark, alarm that already covers the satiation point makes the machine climb, unless fighting is costly or there are enough communities to dissolve the alarm at the stopping point.

None of this shows that these conditions are necessary for restraint.

Part 9. In the model, whether a satisfied machine stops depends on safety, cost and humanity’s choices

The model turns a broad hope, that a satisfied superintelligence would stop expanding, into the five questions of Part 1.

On the first, stopping against a given strike risk is the best policy exactly when the weighted gain from moving up one fort and doing the best from there is no more than one attack’s cost. In the one-step gain, satiation removes the goal part and leaves the safety part intact.

On the second, suppose there is no threat and, from the next fort onward, each successive fort adds no more to the goal than the previous one added. Then the stopping version of the heartland condition gives the rate of decline needed for a stop. A patient enough machine does not stop while the next fort still adds anything.

On the third, the conjecture examined in Ends, Rank and Conflict is tested here in a narrower form: whether a satiable goal makes stopping best against a given strike risk. In the model, it splits into three cases:

  • stopping is best at every attack cost under Theorem A’s conditions, when more holdings do not lower the risk;
  • stopping is not best at any cost below the blocking cost, under Theorem C’s conditions;
  • at or above the blocking cost, the basic test decides; in the computed example, the satiated machine stops at holding 3 at attack costs of 0.563 or more when strikes come one period in ten.

On the fourth, a calm stopping point with no rivals lets a satiated machine stop at any cost. Both sides stop from the satiation point up in the peace profile when no community gains from striking. In the dynamic game, peace at the satiation point needs only the strike conditions at that holding.

On the fifth, adding communities dissolves an imperfect, costly plug coalition. Yet under the fixed-propensity benchmark, independent rival building blocks stopping below a positive attack cost. With symmetric strategic rivals, where all communities follow the same rival strategy, the dynamic game gives two examples:

  • In the alarm example, a community’s stake in removal at holding 3 is 10, a rival’s chance of success there is about 0.171, building one costs 1, and patience is 0.9. A rival’s chance times the stake, about 1.714, exceeds its cost of 1. So the peace condition for rivals fails at holding 3, which leaves a positive blocking cost for sixteen or more communities. In this example the block includes attack costs of one-half or less.
  • In the calm example, the stake is 1, so a rival’s chance times the stake is about 0.171, below the cost of 1. For two or more communities, peace at holding 3 is one equilibrium at every attack cost. Uniqueness is not shown, and attack equilibria are not ruled out.

A Test the Conjecture Could Lose, my paper designing empirical tests of these conditions, aims to estimate when security motives override a satiable goal. Those tests have not been run. Which set of conditions describes any real machine or any real human communities is not settled here and remains a conjecture.

The exceptional human minds examined in Ends, Rank and Conflict were rarely able to fight cheaply against all of humanity. Their record is therefore weak evidence on the safety part, and I rest nothing on it.

Finally, the results flag, but do not assert, a design implication for the institutional measures in Measures That Depend on Ends, my paper on measures that depend on what a machine wants. It applies if humanity relies on coordinated tripwires and the satiation point can be verified:

  • Making alarm depend on expansion beyond the satiation point (as in Table 1) can support an equilibrium stop at holding 3 for a few communities. Attack equilibria can coexist at the same cost.
  • With alarm at or below the satiation point (as in Table 2), among the numbers of communities in Table 2, only with one community does every computed equilibrium climb from holding 3 at attack costs below 1.045. For two, four and eight communities, alarm-driven climbs coexist with stops that hold even when attacking is free. Equilibria in which players choose at random (mixed equilibria) that coexist with these non-random ones are not classified.

Part 10. What the model does not claim, and what would change the answer

The other side is given, not derived. In the first half of the technical paper, the opponent is a fixed strike risk. In the second, the communities’ payoffs, strike costs and chances of success are taken as given, not derived from some deeper game. In all the stopping problems before the dynamic game, “stopping is the best policy” means best against a strike risk taken as given.

No bargaining is modelled. Smith and Stam (2001) ask whether both sides would prefer a peaceful handover of forts to war. I ask only when stopping pays.

Conflict is simplified. A strike either fails and changes nothing or ends the machine; there is no partial damage. The machine loses no forts when its own attack fails, and holdings change one fort at a time. The machine is neutral to risk, and both sides share the same fixed patience. Satiation is a flow enjoyed while alive, with defeat worth zero, not a finished goal kept after defeat. Information is complete: nobody is unsure of the machine’s goals or satiation point, and nobody learns about odds or costs from fighting (Smith and Stam 2004, 2005).

The checking has a stated scope. The analytical results up to the dynamic game are checked in Lean 4, subject to recorded conditions and exceptions:

  • Whether the best holding-only rule remains best among broader rules is checked for rules that depend on the machine’s history, for finite mixtures of rules, and for humanity’s rules that assign weights to actions while the machine stays put.
  • The remark on the reverse order of events is checked only when strikes happen, the fixed value of going on is positive, and the next fort lowers a strike’s chance of success.
  • The Lean check of the break-even cost threshold under a strict rule for ties assumes that the break-even cost is positive.
  • The selection rule enters the first and third tripwire results as an assumption.
  • The numerical examples and both tables are computed by scripts.
  • The step from Theorem P’s two checked halves to an equilibrium at every point of the game from the satiation point on is a hand proof.

The dynamic game has its own assumptions. Its equilibrium results are computed or proved on paper. They let the machine advance after a failed strike when it chooses to attack, and they make the attack decision at the same time as the decisions to strike. Throughout the second half, everyone sees all actions and outcomes, but the equilibria depend only on the current holding. When testing whether a player can gain by changing its strategy, that player may also use the history of play. That rules out machine retaliation after failed strikes and human alarm after failed attacks. Equilibria that depend on history are not characterised.

The tripwire tables are benchmarks. They use a game in which communities choose only whether to pull, hold stakes fixed, and pick everyone pulling wherever that is an equilibrium. The dynamic game revisits them by setting per-period payoffs from those stakes and treating strategic rival building separately.

Nothing has been measured. The model has one machine facing humanity; interactions among several machines belong to Many Machines. Nothing here has been measured on actual AI systems or societies. Whether a machine’s goals can be made satiable, and stay satiable as it modifies itself, is a limit I examine in Limits, and an Answer. Where human alarm would begin, and how many communities would have to agree to pull a plug, are conjectures too.

What would change the answer. Several extensions could:

  • allowing communities to follow different rival strategies, and letting rival projects persist;
  • allowing strikes to cause partial losses, or allowing failed attacks to risk losing forts or attacks themselves to provoke a higher strike risk (either of the last two could shrink or remove Theorem C’s blocking cost);
  • adding learning during war;
  • moving to a world of many machines.

Part 11. What to take away

In this model, a machine that wants only so much faces a one-step test: stop when moving up one fort, and doing the best from there, is not worth one attack. With no threat, the appetite for more must fall low enough, and a patient enough machine keeps going while the next fort adds anything.

Satiation removes the goal part of the gain from one more fort but leaves the safety part. When more holdings buy no safety, satiation is enough at any cost. When they buy safety without intermediate peril, the satiated goal is worth something, defeat is not certain, and domination ends or lowers the threat, cheap fighting blocks stopping, though a high enough attack cost still lets the machine stop.

When humanity chooses in holding-only play, peace needs no community to gain from striking on its own at the stopping point. Adding communities of fixed capability dissolves an imperfect, costly plug coalition under bounded stakes, while rivals that need only one keep a threat alive under a fixed positive building propensity and depend on payoffs once strategic. Tripwires help only in some cases. The study uses no measurements from actual AI systems or societies.

Where to read more

  • Satiation Is Not Enough, the technical paper: the formal definitions, exact conditions, proofs and computed tables, with a record of which claims are machine-checked.
  • The War Baseline: the commitment problem, the chain-of-forts model, the heartland condition, and the assumption that humanity cannot promise never to build a rival.
  • Ends, Rank and Conflict: the debate over whether actors with limited aims can rest satisfied, the conjecture tested here, and the record of exceptional human minds.
  • Many Machines: interactions among several machines, including a rival that puts a new machine in charge.
  • A Test the Conjecture Could Lose: the design of empirical tests of these conditions, not yet run.
  • Measures That Depend on Ends: the institutional measures for which a design implication about tripwires is flagged.
  • Limits, and an Answer: whether a machine’s goals can be made satiable and stay so under self-modification.
